newsitem.title: MEXICO: Lawmakers find $1.3 billion hole in Mexican accounts.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers find $1.3 billion hole in Mexican accounts.

text.p: Mexican lawmakers said on Friday $1.34 billion was missing from the 1990 privatization of Mexico's phone company, Telefonos de Mexico, and that they found thousands of other anomalies in a public audit of the last year of ex-President Carlos Salinas' government.

The Mexican press denounced the missing cash in banner headlines and speculated that officials may have carried on a murky tradition in 1994 of stuffing pockets with public funds just before the president's six-year-term came to a close.
But the congressmen who pointed out the anomalies also said the money may have been misplaced due to accounting errors and could show up eventually as other audits were carried out.

"This is a problem of where the (funds) are registered for accounting purposes," Congressman Marco Antonio Michel of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), a secretary of the Finance Oversight Committee, said on national radio.
"The resources (from phone company Telefonos de Mexico) did enter the public purse, but they were not registered," he said.
The committee issued a report on Thursday after auditing only 10 percent of 1994 public accounts that found 3,089 iregularities in 552 cases.

"There are irregularities of all kinds," said committee President Juan Antonio Garcia Villa of the opposition National Action Party (PAN). For example, some 400 million pesos ($54 million) were unaccounted for that had been earmarked for public works projects, he said.
An audit of federal funds transferred to schools -- one of the most costly items in the budget -- was also not possible because accounts had not been made available, he added.

The doubts about the missing Telefonos de Mexico, or Telmex, funds -- a part of the $6 billion the phone monopoly made when it was sold into private hands -- add to a growing controversy about the entire privatization process that won Salinas plaudits all over the world in the early 1990s.
The ex-president fled into voluntary exile three months after leaving office in December 1994 when his brother Raul was arrested on murder and embezzlement charges.

Opposition congressmen have pressed for an investigation into allegations that Raul Salinas, who has been accused of amassing hundreds of millions of dollars while his brother ruled the country, may have accepted kickbacks to help his friends buy privatized firms.

The congressmen held out hope that the missing funds would be accounted for by the time they finish their audit in 45 days. They said the Finance Ministry was responsible for clearing up many of the doubts. Finance Ministry officials were not immediately available for comment.
The missing funds have fanned an already heated debate in Congress about allegations of corruption during the 1988-94 Salinas administration.
On Wednesday, PRI deputies shut down a probe into past accounts at the subsidized food distribution agency Conasupo that led to charges of a coverup by the opposition.
The PRI, the party of President Ernesto Zedillo, has ruled Mexico for 67 years and was largely unsupervised until recently when opposition parties like the PAN began gaining more clout in Congress.
